## Unpacking representation bias, one simulation at a time

Electoral institutions are hard to study causally with real-world data: malapportionment, district magnitude, the seat-allocation formula and the legal threshold are jointly determined, endogenous, and rarely vary independently of one another in any single country. *Unpacking Representation Bias: A Simulation Approach to Electoral Institutions* (Guinjoan, Carbonell &amp; Rogers) sidesteps this problem by simulating large numbers of synthetic polities — up to 10,000 runs per exercise — in which each institutional parameter is introduced **exogenously and independently** of the others, and validating the resulting decomposition against real data from Spain's 2019 European Parliament election.

This is where **MRB**, **SRB**, **ThRB** and **TRB** — introduced on the [Malapportionment Bias](malapportionment-bias.qmd) page — are actually separated out:

- **Malapportionment** generates the **MRB**.
- **District magnitude** and the **seat-allocation formula**, jointly, generate the **SRB**.
- The **legal electoral threshold** generates the **ThRB**.
- The three together sum to the **TRB**, the total gap between the electorate's ideological centre and that of the elected legislature.

### Headline findings

- Malapportionment bias is generally **modest under random territorial imbalance**, but can become substantial when malapportionment is **ideologically concentrated**.
- **SRB is consistently the dominant source of distortion** across the full empirically relevant range of district magnitudes — echoing the [Origins of Institutions](origins.qmd) finding that district-level rules, not malapportionment alone, do most of the work.
- Legal thresholds generate **meaningful bias only at levels well above common European practice**.
- All three components **scale with party-system polarization and fragmentation**.
